source: Per-50 AUTEUR render MAP OS deltas from Codex vision workers

examples.rule: Add an explicit minimum motion contract for video outputs.
examples.when_to_use: Pack shots, office b-roll, landscape plates, and any prompt vulnerable to becoming a still image.
examples.why_it_matters: HydraTrack and office-monitor renders were competent stills but failed as videos because the sampled frames showed almost no meaningful change.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Minimum Motion Validator

examples.rule: Add an identity lock for named species, vehicles, ingredients, and repeated characters.
examples.when_to_use: When semantic identity is more specific than a generic visual class.
examples.why_it_matters: Generic broad leaves replaced curry-leaf sprigs, Rafale geometry drifted, and repeated deity or character identities changed across frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Reference-Conditioned Identity Lock with semantic QC

examples.rule: Add semantic exclusion and object-conservation guards between adjacent shots.
examples.when_to_use: Batch generation, transformations, montage prompts, and sequences with persistent props.
examples.why_it_matters: A repeated slogan-wearing person contaminated watch outputs, symbolic objects replaced an eagle sequence, and a coffee cup vanished during a cookie transformation.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Cross-shot Contamination and Conservation Checker

examples.rule: Allow shape transformation only when the design system is nonliteral and its palette, line weight, and motion grammar are explicitly locked.
examples.when_to_use: Abstract motion graphics, floral morphs, neon geometry, and other nonrepresentational animation.
examples.why_it_matters: Transformation became an asset in the best abstract renders but a defect in faces, geography, products, and architecture.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Transformation permission matrix by content type, with immutable semantic anchors.

examples.rule: Apply a visible-beat complexity budget and split prompts when the requested environments, eras, products, actions, or title cards exceed one generation unit.
examples.when_to_use: Multi-era morphs, 20-25 second extreme-sport montages, software promos, or prompts with many timestamp blocks.
examples.why_it_matters: Decade morphs collapsed to one outfit; APEX variants omitted several scenes; Runway promos produced unreadable collage walls instead of controlled interface beats.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prompt complexity meter that converts overloaded prompts into shot cards and reports deferred constraints.

examples.rule: Assign one action owner and one oversized scale anchor before adding secondary characters.
examples.when_to_use: Miniature cooking, hand-scale fantasy, product demonstrations, and any forced-perspective scene.
examples.why_it_matters: Single-chef hand and leaf scenes kept scale and action readable; crowded miniature scenes let human hands, giant knives, or inconsistent chef sizes take over.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Action-ownership and scale-hierarchy pass that labels actor, tool, target, anchor, and forbidden human intervention.

examples.rule: Avoid hands unless the action can be staged with a single visible grip and stable contact geometry.
examples.when_to_use: Opening chests, sprinkling particles, raising drinks, or touching luxury products.
examples.why_it_matters: Hand-heavy clips showed anatomy, object-contact, and continuity failures that were absent from camera-driven reveals.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Human Interaction risk toggle with No Hands default

examples.rule: Bind a hero identity or object across shots before adding geography or action variety.
examples.when_to_use: Human narratives and automotive montages with more than one shot.
examples.why_it_matters: Identity and vehicle continuity failed when prompts prioritized many locations and beats without a continuity budget.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Hero-lock block with immutable identity, wardrobe/body, color/model, and maximum shot count.

examples.rule: Bind aspect ratio and active-image occupancy as explicit delivery constraints, not only prompt tokens.
examples.when_to_use: All generated video, especially horizontal outputs consumed in vertical containers.
examples.why_it_matters: Several nominally horizontal action/watch renders arrived as portrait crops or extremely thin letterboxed strips.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Active Image Ratio Gate

examples.rule: Bind prompt audio events to render capability before dispatch.
examples.when_to_use: Prompts where a roar, impact, speech line, music cue, or synchronized sound is the primary event.
examples.why_it_matters: Every Mercedes-AMG prompt defined a V8 roar, while every corresponding metadata record declared has_audio=false.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Audio Capability Gate with visual-only rewrite or audio-enabled route selection.

examples.rule: Break ignition prompts into visible pre-strike, contact/spark, ignition transfer, and sustained-flame states.
examples.when_to_use: Matches, tandoors, cocktails, candles, and other fire transformations.
examples.why_it_matters: The batch frequently jumped from an unlit tool to a full flame, skipped sparks, or produced oversized ribbon-like fire.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Ignition-state prompt builder with temporal phase locks and flame-scale constraints.

examples.rule: Budget five-second prompts as two visibly testable beats with one primary action per beat and an explicit transition verb.
examples.when_to_use: Dual-scene narrative prompts and cause-to-payoff sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Many renders preserved the attractive setup but omitted the failure cascade, smartwatch, neighbor reveal, or dissolution payoff.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Duration-aware beat allocator with mandatory beat-coverage checks.

examples.rule: Budget no more than three visually distinct beats for a five-second render and reserve the final beat for the payoff.
examples.when_to_use: Short product ads and transformation spots.
examples.why_it_matters: FitFuel prompts requested stress, sachet, dissolve, light shift, sip, focus change, cursor, overlay, and logo; most renders omitted or reordered beats.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Duration-aware Beat Budget validator with required endpoint reservation.

examples.rule: Budget one clearly visible action beat per five-second render; split multi-beat ads into separate shots before generation.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt containing retrieval, opening, pouring, macro insert, drinking, lighting transformation, posture change, and logo reveal in one short clip.
examples.why_it_matters: The FitFuel renders captured only one partial beat and omitted the transformation, while long butter-chicken renders introduced unrelated late scenes.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Duration-aware beat budgeter that rejects or auto-splits over-scripted prompts.

examples.rule: Budget one continuous subject identity, environment, and physical action per generation; route multi-location concepts to explicit shot cards.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt that combines multiple locations, scales, characters, or conceptual domains inside 10-15 seconds.
examples.why_it_matters: Overloaded renders produced disappearing cars, disconnected molecular imagery, and anatomy changes, while focused studio, tunnel, and craft actions stayed coherent.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Temporal complexity meter that recommends split-shot generation when subject, location, or physics budgets are exceeded.

examples.rule: Budget one readable beat per available two seconds and reject timestamp blocks that exceed the rendered duration.
examples.when_to_use: For multi-beat action prompts and long structured scene specifications.
examples.why_it_matters: The 8-second aircraft arc was rendered in 5 seconds and collapsed to one rolling maneuver, while the 10-second miniature-chef render alone achieved setup, action, and result coverage.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Duration-Aware Beat Budgeter

examples.rule: Budget prompts around five to seven visually provable beats; demote unsupported camera, physics, and audio micro-specifications.
examples.when_to_use: Any 10-15 second generation with dense technical prose or second-by-second action.
examples.why_it_matters: The batch repeatedly rendered the broad subject while dropping fine mechanics, producing prompt bloat without visible control.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prompt Beat Budget with visible must-have versus optional constraints.

examples.rule: Cap simultaneous human interactions and stage contacts in isolated beats before adding crowds, water, or impacts.
examples.when_to_use: Fights, disaster scenes, rescues, and dense crowd action.
examples.why_it_matters: Complex contact scenes produced merged limbs, identity drift, and physics breaks even when their environments looked strong.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Human-interaction complexity budget with staged-contact templates.

examples.rule: Cap simultaneous micro-physics subjects and assign a visibility priority to every required element.
examples.when_to_use: Scientific macro, material interaction, underwater, particle, or multi-object VFX prompts.
examples.why_it_matters: The five-material underwater prompts rendered striking imagery but could not keep all elements identifiable and stable at once.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Complexity Budget with required-element visibility ranking

examples.rule: Colossal scale prompts require explicit tiny reference subjects in the frame.
examples.when_to_use: Giants, vehicles, architecture, disasters, planets, and monster scenes.
examples.why_it_matters: Scale was strongest when tiny people appeared near the giant and weakest when the giant stood alone.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Scale-lock control that inserts reference figures, distance, and foreground/background size relationships.

examples.rule: Compile a protected subject-action tuple before expanding style language.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt whose commercial or narrative identity depends on one actor performing one action.
examples.why_it_matters: The golden-hour walking prompt became cycling in one render, and several miniature-worker prompts became full-size human actions.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Subject-action lock with post-render mismatch flags.

examples.rule: Compile a visible state bridge for every material transformation.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt where beans, powder, liquid, smoke, fabric, or another material must become or enter a new state.
examples.why_it_matters: Coffee variants jumped from intact beans to pre-existing liquid or a later pour, and spice particles became floating ribbons instead of completing a credible source-contact-result chain.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Transformation compiler with source state, contact event, intermediate state, destination state, and forbidden substitution fields.

examples.rule: Compile aspect ratio, duration, audio, exact text, camera angle, and defining action into hard render constraints before prose styling.
examples.when_to_use: Whenever a prompt includes explicit output geometry, timed beats, sound, typography, or a named camera setup.
examples.why_it_matters: Eighteen records ignored aspect instructions, twelve lacked requested audio intent, and text-heavy cosmic renders produced malformed copy despite strong visual style.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Hard Constraint Compiler with pre-render conflict and capability checks

examples.rule: Compile each requested storyboard beat as a separately named shot with required subject, action, entry state, exit state, and minimum visibility.
examples.when_to_use: Montages, transformations, rituals, and any prompt containing three or more narrative beats.
examples.why_it_matters: AI-insights variants collapsed five beats into one or two graphics, while the structured automotive montage delivered runway, human bridge, and residential payoff.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat Coverage Contract with required-shot checklist

examples.rule: Compile every multi-character prompt with immutable subject IDs, roles, wardrobe, and a do-not-merge constraint.
examples.when_to_use: Any sequence with two or more people, an AI entity plus a human, or a human-to-particle transition.
examples.why_it_matters: Unbound identities produced duplicate bodies, extra characters, entity-human morphing, and dissolution of the wrong subject.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Character continuity compiler with role locks and transition ownership.

examples.rule: Compile exact brand text and logos into a post-render typography layer instead of asking the video model to draw them.
examples.when_to_use: Any branded product, launch card, logo reveal, cup mark, dial, clasp, or headline.
examples.why_it_matters: Visible text was absent, substituted, or gibberish across watch, coffee, restaurant-title, and AI-launch renders even when the underlying composition was strong.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Render-safe text compiler that emits a clean plate plus deterministic typography/logo overlay instructions.

examples.rule: Compile explicit identity invariants before style language: subject face, garment pattern, vehicle silhouette, bottle geometry, cap, label, and logo spelling.
examples.when_to_use: Reference-led fashion, branded products, recurring vehicles, or any multi-shot sequence.
examples.why_it_matters: Models changed identity, dresses simplified, APEX bottles changed shape and spelling, and automotive body details drifted between angles.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity-lock block with reference anchors, invariant checksum, and allowed-variation fields.

examples.rule: Compile immutable hero identity anchors before camera or motion tokens: exact object topology, color, count, text, and identifying marks must persist through every beat.
examples.when_to_use: Branded products, vehicles, recurring characters, and historically specific subjects.
examples.why_it_matters: The plate-anchored Mustang stayed coherent while watches repeatedly changed crowns, dials, hands, and even ceased to be watches.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity Lock block with immutable attributes and per-beat continuity assertions

examples.rule: Compile multi-beat prompts into a duration-budgeted must-show checklist before generation.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt with three or more sequential actions, a location change, or a required ending.
examples.why_it_matters: Domestic, travel, future-camera, fashion, and launch prompts repeatedly delivered attractive fragments while omitting the causal middle or final beat.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat Budget Compiler with must-show, optional, and forbidden beat slots

examples.rule: Compile named characters and branded products from an identity anchor before adding mood or camera language.
examples.when_to_use: Recurring people, watches, androids, logos, and props across a sequence.
examples.why_it_matters: Ashley changed ethnicity and facial identity; watch engravings and hardware changed; android bodies changed from humanlike to visibly mechanical.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity-lock block with reference image, invariant traits, allowed variations, and continuity checksum.

examples.rule: Compile short visible beat contracts before adding technical camera or material detail.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt with more than one scene, transformation, or product reveal.
examples.why_it_matters: Cafe and alley variants rendered complete stories when each sampled beat had one obvious subject-action-purpose pair; extreme physics and fifteen-scene prompts frequently collapsed or substituted a single scene.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat-contract compiler that emits subject, action, camera, continuity anchor, and proof frame for every beat.

examples.rule: Constrain one visible material behavior per macro prompt before adding camera telemetry.
examples.when_to_use: Liquid, food, ice, smoke, fabric, particles, or other physics-led close-ups.
examples.why_it_matters: The cleanest renders mapped a simple physical cause to a readable temporal progression; large numerical spec blocks did not prevent steam, geometry, or continuity failures.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Material behavior selector with cause, progression, failure guard, and end-state fields.

examples.rule: Constrain saturation, highlight clipping, and shadow floor explicitly for neon cities and sunsets.
examples.when_to_use: Night-city, tropical-sunset, and high-contrast desert scenes.
examples.why_it_matters: Several clips retained composition but lost trust through clipped color, crushed silhouettes, neon overprocessing, or exposure collapse.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Look-density controls for saturation ceiling, highlight rolloff, and minimum shadow detail.

examples.rule: Constrain vapor with source, rise direction, maximum plume scale, opacity, and no-liquid-intersection guards.
examples.when_to_use: For coffee, food, or atmospheric prompts where steam is a hero motion element.
examples.why_it_matters: Unconstrained steam often became cloth-like ribbons, descended into liquid, or overwhelmed the vessel.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Vapor physics guardrail preset

examples.rule: Convert long prompts into a small ordered set of non-negotiable visual gates before adding texture language.
examples.when_to_use: Multi-beat action, transformation, or scale-dependent concepts.
examples.why_it_matters: The jet sequence retained mood but lost missile, flare, and near-miss beats; the fashion sequence skipped eras; the miniature workers lost scale entirely.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Required-beat compiler with a maximum active-constraint budget per shot.

examples.rule: Convert negative constraints into post-render checks instead of assuming the prompt alone enforces them.
examples.when_to_use: Brand-safe products, watches, charts, UI, and any prompt forbidding text, logos, morphing, or static output.
examples.why_it_matters: No-logo, no-text, and motion requirements still failed visibly despite explicit negative clauses.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Constraint-to-validator compiler that emits text, logo, geometry, and frame-delta checks.

examples.rule: Convert prohibitions about branding, text, hands, or anatomy into explicit frame-QC gates rather than relying on negative wording alone.
examples.when_to_use: Branded products, mobile interfaces, craft hands, and animal locomotion.
examples.why_it_matters: Readable Chanel labeling, synthetic app icons, unstable fingers, and ambiguous hoof gait survived prompt-level prohibitions or absent intent.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Pre-export visual lint for readable marks, UI glyph validity, hand anatomy, and gait continuity.

examples.rule: Convert screenplay prose into a bounded beat list and reserve exact typography for a deterministic post-render title pass.
examples.when_to_use: Trailers, teasers, title-card sequences, and prompts containing more than five narrative beats or exact slogans.
examples.why_it_matters: Long trailer prompts compressed unpredictably, omitted most scenes, and produced gibberish slogans even when the main title sometimes rendered correctly.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Trailer Beat Compiler plus deterministic title-card renderer.

examples.rule: Declare an entity budget and keep miniature-animal shots to one hero or two separated subjects.
examples.when_to_use: Rabbit, mascot, pet, and other creature scenes with oversized environments.
examples.why_it_matters: Single- and two-subject shots retained identity and geography; crowded gardens repeatedly produced count, scale, and anatomy drift.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Entity Budget and Occlusion Guard

examples.rule: Declare brand policy before generation: licensed mark, de-branded silhouette, or fictional identity.
examples.when_to_use: Automotive, restaurant, packaged product, and fashion work.
examples.why_it_matters: Visible badges, labels, plates, and invented overlays repeatedly damaged otherwise strong renders.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Brand Safety mode with logo, plate, label, and overlay guards.

examples.rule: Declare hero-detail invariants in the prompt: the latte pattern, liquid level, label, garnish, and character identity must remain unchanged across every frame.
examples.when_to_use: Close-ups where a high-frequency surface pattern or small character carries the shot.
examples.why_it_matters: Latte motifs redrew themselves, coffee surfaces developed bubbles without cause, and miniature identities changed despite stable camera setups.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Temporal-invariant prompt block with object-level locks.

examples.rule: Declare immutable identity anchors for faces, products, wardrobe, and props at every angle or scale transition.
examples.when_to_use: Watch or automotive orbit shots, multi-angle people, age transformations, and any sequence where exact identity matters.
examples.why_it_matters: Watch dials, bracelets, car bodies, faces, beards, and backpacks repeatedly changed between sampled frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Continuity-lock block that serializes reference identity, fixed geometry, wardrobe, accessories, and prohibited changes.

examples.rule: Declare observable first, transition, and final states for every essential temporal event, and require each state to remain visible long enough to verify.
examples.when_to_use: Ignitions, product transformations, entrances, exits, pours, drifts, and any prompt whose value depends on a state change.
examples.why_it_matters: Many renders produced attractive final-state imagery while omitting the ignition, look-back, assembly, recovery, or other defining transition.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Temporal State Contract with required start/transition/end checkpoints

examples.rule: Declare one immutable prop ontology and state sequence for short-form product actions.
examples.when_to_use: Ingredient handling, opening, pouring, transferring, or presenting a product container.
examples.why_it_matters: Containers changed among jar, mug, handled vessel, and tin, while lids and contents appeared or transformed.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prop-state lock with start-state, allowed transitions, and forbidden geometry changes.

examples.rule: Declare one mandatory proof frame for the central physical action and reject outputs that only imply it.
examples.when_to_use: Stunts, transformations, impacts, workflow demos, and any cause-effect sequence.
examples.why_it_matters: Two rooftop prompts omitted the defining leap, while the successful facade variant showed the airborne body in a locked wide and the catch in a separate payoff frame.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Mandatory Proof Beat validator

examples.rule: Declare scale ownership: miniature characters must perform the hero action unless human intervention is explicitly requested.
examples.when_to_use: Miniature-worker, tiny-chef, diorama, or giant-ingredient frameworks.
examples.why_it_matters: Full-size hands repeatedly took over pouring, moving, seasoning, or lifting and caused character displacement and scale drift.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Scale-ownership parameter: autonomous-miniature, mixed-scale-reveal, or human-assisted.

examples.rule: Default to no visible text or branding unless exact copy and placement are supplied as locked assets.
examples.when_to_use: Packaging, signs, uniforms, vehicles, and machinery.
examples.why_it_matters: Uncontrolled labels became pseudo-logos or gibberish even when the surrounding render was visually credible.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Text-risk preflight that routes exact copy to a compositing or locked-asset pass.

examples.rule: Define immutable identity anchors before requesting any orbital or multi-angle product showcase.
examples.when_to_use: Watches, bottles, vehicles and any object whose value depends on exact geometry, text or model fidelity.
examples.why_it_matters: This batch repeatedly preserved category while changing date windows, dials, necks, logos, headlights or body seams across angles.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity Lock block with reference frame, silhouette anchors, countable details, protected text zones and reject-on-drift validation.

examples.rule: Define the final visible payoff as a non-optional last-frame condition.
examples.when_to_use: Use for pours, awakenings, expression fixes, reveals, greetings, and activation sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Many renders established a strong setup but omitted the requested smile, eye opening, insertion, greeting, or loop closure.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Mandatory payoff frame field with validator against sampled final frames.

examples.rule: Describe a product's immutable geometry and material layers before describing any transformation or reveal.
examples.when_to_use: Drinkware, packaging, and other isolated product renders.
examples.why_it_matters: Without explicit identity anchors, cup height, rim shape, opacity, and internal layers drift between frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Product identity lock with geometry, material, and transparency fields.

examples.rule: Describe a stable identity token before requesting rapid location changes.
examples.when_to_use: Any montage that must preserve one product, vehicle or person across cuts.
examples.why_it_matters: A repeated color, silhouette and hero-detail lock made the yellow Porsche and black mug legible; unbounded coastal-car prompts swapped models and paint.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity Lock block with color, silhouette, hero detail and forbidden-drift fields.

examples.rule: Describe measurable UI semantics as a small fixed field set and prohibit decorative microcopy.
examples.when_to_use: Biometric, system-status, and AI-analysis interfaces.
examples.why_it_matters: Dense dashboards obscured the requested cortisol, oxytocin, sleep, and health outcomes behind unreadable labels and invalid percentages.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Schema-backed UI prompt compiler with metric name, unit, range, and direction.

examples.rule: Describe one visible causal action per beat, then allocate a dedicated proof frame for the result.
examples.when_to_use: Product demos, brewing, storage transformations, vehicle launches, and physical fights.
examples.why_it_matters: Simple Caraway, coffee, motorcycle, and traffic beats remained legible; dense fight and multi-action prompts produced smeared anatomy, unclear contact, or missing states.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat Causality And Proof Builder

examples.rule: Describe transparent bubbles with bounded diameter, separation, refraction, and no-fusion constraints.
examples.when_to_use: Underwater macro, liquid aeration, foam, and effervescence shots.
examples.why_it_matters: Unbounded macro bubbles became chrome-like rocks or fused solid chains instead of transparent gas pockets.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Fluid-material guardrail presets for bubble scale, transparency, deformation, rise speed, and allowed coalescence.

examples.rule: Disambiguate polysemous production nouns before prompt expansion; compile 'elevator car' as 'elevator cabin (not an automobile)' when architecture is intended.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt containing car, crane, shot, plate, track, model, or other terms with competing film, object, and domain meanings.
examples.why_it_matters: Two luxury-elevator prompts produced automobiles because the expanded prompt repeatedly used 'elevator car' without a negative semantic guard.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Semantic ambiguity linter with selectable noun sense and auto-generated negative guards.

examples.rule: Do not ask the renderer to produce business-critical exact text unless a compositing repair lane is selected.
examples.when_to_use: Brand facades, charts, signs, packaging, uniforms, documents, and dashboards.
examples.why_it_matters: Prominent requested copy repeatedly became misspelled, malformed, unstable, or unreadable even when the surrounding image was strong.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Text-Risk guard that routes exact copy to post-render overlay or rejects text-dependent generation.

examples.rule: Do not blend unrelated shots unless a shared material, scale, and transformation path are explicitly storyboarded.
examples.when_to_use: Montages, match cuts, food transformations, and multi-scene blends.
examples.why_it_matters: The syrup-to-fire blends jumped between macro liquid and differently scaled chefs with no spatial or material bridge.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Transition Contract with from-state, bridge material, scale lock, and to-state.

examples.rule: Do not request an unconstrained continuous identity morph; stage the transformation through verified age checkpoints or cuts.
examples.when_to_use: Anti-aging, metamorphosis, character-age, and before-after beauty concepts.
examples.why_it_matters: The continuous age-reversal test collapsed facial anatomy and resolved into a different person.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Transformation planner with identity embeddings, age checkpoints, cut-safe transitions, and a fail-closed face-consistency gate.

examples.rule: Do not use precise numeric performance claims without a visible verification beat.
examples.when_to_use: Automotive, finance, technical and scientific prompts.
examples.why_it_matters: A Tesla performance sequence displayed 9 km/h and a Sea-to-Sky sequence asserted 400 km/h in an implausible public-road context.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Claim Proof mode that converts unsupported numbers into qualitative performance language or requires a matching instrument frame.

examples.rule: Emotional or expression prompts must define visibly distinct facial checkpoints and the exact frame beat that proves each state.
examples.when_to_use: Reaction videos, robot expression tests, reflective portraits, and loneliness-to-hope arcs.
examples.why_it_matters: Robot faces and the gaming reaction remained nearly static, while gaze direction and shot progression communicated emotion more reliably in the umbrella and mirror scenes.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Expression Beat Matrix with neutral, transition, target-state, and hold-duration controls.

examples.rule: Encode miniature scale with explicit comparative anchors and forbid full-size hands unless requested.
examples.when_to_use: Miniature-worker, diorama, model-shop, or tiny-craftsperson scenes.
examples.why_it_matters: Every android-craft variant replaced four 1/24-scale specialists with one normal-size human hand.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Scale Anchor preset with actor-count and forbidden-object constraints

examples.rule: Every lift, fold, garnish, pour, or reveal must name the visible cause and maintain object count.
examples.when_to_use: Food action shots and hand interactions.
examples.why_it_matters: Unsupported levitation, materialization, and unexplained arrangement changes were common failure modes.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Action Causality field requiring actor, tool, start state, end state, and object-count lock.

examples.rule: Every video prompt must name at least one observable subject-motion change, one camera-motion change, and a verifiable end state; otherwise route it as a still-life request.
examples.when_to_use: Short product prompts for cups, espresso glasses, jars, packaging, or any scene that could be satisfied by one static frame.
examples.why_it_matters: Fifteen records were effectively static, while prompts with explicit action stages produced more useful temporal craft.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Motion Intent Guard that requires subject_motion, camera_motion, and end_state fields before video generation.

examples.rule: Express action direction explicitly with start state, transition verb, and end state.
examples.when_to_use: Reversible prop actions such as put on/remove, open/close, approach/withdraw, or reveal/conceal.
examples.why_it_matters: Two Park Guell variants put on or adjusted sunglasses when the prompt required removal, while variants with visible start and end states performed the action correctly.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Action-polarity guard

examples.rule: Express identity as visible invariants and explicitly forbid category substitution.
examples.when_to_use: Use when human versus android, crown versus gear, or a specific food morphology is essential.
examples.why_it_matters: Human androids became metallic robots, watch crowns became free-standing gears, and gulab jamun surfaces became faceted or flower-like.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Subject-invariant block with positive identifiers and negative exclusions.

examples.rule: Express immutable identity and object state explicitly across every beat.
examples.when_to_use: Human close-ups, branded products, vehicles, architecture, and multi-shot sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Faces, hair, cigarettes, vehicle panels, labels, and hidden-city states drifted even when visual quality was high.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Continuity ledger that repeats immutable subject, wardrobe, prop, geometry, and environment state per beat.

examples.rule: Express one claim with one visible proof object or action per beat.
examples.when_to_use: Use for short-form comedy, product benefits, app-connected devices, and escalation montages.
examples.why_it_matters: Coffee, phone, doorway, garment, and app beats remained legible when each frame had one narrative job.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat-proof planner with a required visible-evidence field for every storyboard beat.

examples.rule: Express physical actions as visible state transitions: start state, contact, transformation, and end state.
examples.when_to_use: Food preparation, stunt impacts, assembly, and any prompt where causality matters.
examples.why_it_matters: Mood language alone produced attractive frames but frequent object pop-in, impossible material changes, and omitted impact mechanics.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Causal Action State Builder

examples.rule: Express scale through at least two visible comparative anchors, not adjectives alone.
examples.when_to_use: Miniatures, giants, macro worlds, or any concept whose premise depends on relative size.
examples.why_it_matters: All four miniature-worker renders depicted normal-size adults because no ordinary object visibly established 2.5 cm scale.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Scale-anchor selector requiring foreground and background comparison objects.

examples.rule: For a five-second render, default to one hero subject, one environment, one camera move, and one visible action or atmospheric motion cue.
examples.when_to_use: Use for single-shot ads, b-roll, food, product, and short character reveals.
examples.why_it_matters: The 18-character coffee prompt produced the only clean gold render, while multi-thousand-character prompts repeatedly collapsed to one motif and dropped most actions.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Five-second complexity budget with automatic storyboard routing when entity, location, text, or beat counts exceed the budget.

examples.rule: For a five-second timed sequence, define one required visual proof per beat and reject variants that collapse or omit either beat.
examples.when_to_use: Timed sequence prompts with an environment/action beat followed by a reaction, reveal, or cut.
examples.why_it_matters: Jeep, ruin-observer, and library-door variants often rendered only one attractive setup while dropping the aerial, observer, eye close-up, or blackout beat.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat-proof checklist with per-beat frame evidence and a missing-beat rejection flag.

examples.rule: For animal flight or walking, pin species identity, body proportions, travel direction, environment, and one camera path while allowing only physically plausible gait or wing-phase changes.
examples.when_to_use: Wildlife tracking, approach, banking, or profile shots.
examples.why_it_matters: The strongest wildlife clips kept identity and setting stable; weaker variants drifted in tails, paws, feathers, or wing silhouettes.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Wildlife Motion Guard with anatomy anchors and motion-specific negative constraints.

examples.rule: For five-second renders, prefer one anchored tableau, one visible action, and one explicit context cue.
examples.when_to_use: Single-product, culinary, miniature, and BTS shots where inspectability matters more than montage breadth.
examples.why_it_matters: Concise prompts produced stable subjects and complete visible delivery while over-scoped timed prompts often drifted across identities, objects, locations, or beats.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Single-Tableau prompt mode with subject/action/context slots and a visible-proof checklist.

examples.rule: For heritage jewelry, pair the product with one culturally coherent material or architectural context, then finish on an unobstructed hero view.
examples.when_to_use: Indian necklaces, jhumka earrings, and ornate gold jewelry.
examples.why_it_matters: Carved wood, burgundy display fabric, and palace architecture created stronger discovery and scale than isolated black-velvet catalog frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Heritage Context builder with material, display, and architecture tokens

examples.rule: For landmark architecture, explicitly isolate the hero facade and forbid competing side buildings when pure grandeur is the goal.
examples.when_to_use: Landmark establishing shots.
examples.why_it_matters: Facade-filling Sagrada variants were clean and striking; street-canyon variants introduced geometry drift and weakened subject dominance.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Architecture isolation toggle with surrounding-building allowance and geometry-stability priority.

examples.rule: For liquid action, specify the source vessel, continuous source-to-target stream, viscosity, contact point, and resulting surface response.
examples.when_to_use: Pours, spills, splashes, and beverage preparation.
examples.why_it_matters: The strongest pours kept a visible source, stable cup rim, narrow stream, and plausible ripples; the failed spill originated from impossible cup geometry.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Liquid-physics prompt block with source, path, contact, and aftermath controls.

examples.rule: For liquid food macros, hold the hero still for the setup beats and introduce one clearly directed pour only in the payoff beats.
examples.when_to_use: Syrup, sauce, glaze, beverage, and drizzle content.
examples.why_it_matters: The cleanest food exemplars used stable geometry followed by a late, readable syrup action; variants that transformed the food surface scored lower.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Setup-Hold-Pour macro template with contact-point and pooling controls.

examples.rule: For luxury product macro, specify one rigid hero object, one material contrast, one controlled reflection source, and one slow camera move.
examples.when_to_use: Pens, leather goods, watches, and jewelry.
examples.why_it_matters: The strongest renders held geometry stable while specular light and a restrained move created visual development.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Product Macro Builder with object, material, reflection, surface, and move fields.

examples.rule: For macro biology, explicitly lock topology and reduce simultaneous locomotion, focus travel, and body rotation.
examples.when_to_use: Insects, hands, faces, anatomical VFX, or other close subjects where small topology errors are exposed.
examples.why_it_matters: The insect shots looked credible at first glance but legs, antennae, and wings changed shape and count across frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Macro anatomy guard with topology checklist, motion simplification, and close-QC requirement.

examples.rule: For magical material transformation, define a single material state at each beat and an explicit transition mechanism.
examples.when_to_use: Gold dust, liquid metal, sand, particles, and alchemy effects.
examples.why_it_matters: Gold frequently jumped between granules, liquid blobs, fused surfaces, and foam-like clumps without a readable transformation.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Material State Timeline with state, transition, force, and conservation controls.

examples.rule: For material craft, describe setup, transformation mechanism, and finished result instead of naming only the desired object.
examples.when_to_use: Latte art, opening books, package reveals, smoke, steam, fabric, or any transformation whose physics matter.
examples.why_it_matters: Stage-defined pours and book openings yielded readable progression, while underdefined variants produced concentric liquid rings, levitation, or morphing.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Material Action Composer with setup, force, deformation, settling, and final-shape slots.

examples.rule: For miniature animal scenes, lock one or two subject identities, one route, and all hero props; avoid uncontrolled ensemble crossings.
examples.when_to_use: Macro dioramas, toy-scale worlds, cute-animal stories, and tabletop commercials.
examples.why_it_matters: Single-rabbit exploration and two-rabbit traversal stayed clean, while crowded overlaps caused body blending, count ambiguity, and anatomy drift.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Miniature Story mode with subject-count lock, prop lock, route line, and overlap-risk warning.

examples.rule: For miniature human action, stage readable silhouettes at medium or wide scale and avoid hand-dependent contact beats.
examples.when_to_use: Circus, party, painting, and crowd scenes with multiple figures.
examples.why_it_matters: Hands, faces, ropes, cups, tools, and limb contact were the dominant visible failures.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Human Contact Risk control that recommends silhouette, distance, and prop simplification.

examples.rule: For miniature launch shots, combine one vertical hero action with one or two stationary witness figures.
examples.when_to_use: Toy-space scenes that need a complete narrative beat in five seconds.
examples.why_it_matters: The witness anchors scale and continuity while the single ascent keeps motion easy to read and render.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Launch Beat preset with witness count, launch lane, and ascent distance controls.

examples.rule: For movement-led nature and fashion shots, bind one stable environment, one subject action, one camera path, and one motivated light source in the same shot contract.
examples.when_to_use: Golden-hour dance, aerial canopy, macro botanical, and fabric-motion generations.
examples.why_it_matters: The strongest renders preserved geometry while allowing camera, fabric, or body motion to carry the progression.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Single-Shot Motion Contract with environment, action, camera, and light fields

examples.rule: For multi-character drama, declare a fixed cast list, wardrobe color per character, room map, camera axis, and allowed beat transitions before generating coverage.
examples.when_to_use: Household conflict, mediation, and branded narrative sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Many variants retained attractive faces and interiors but lost coherence through abrupt cast, room, viewpoint, or insert changes.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Cast and Continuity Bible generator

examples.rule: For multi-limb or tool-use subjects, enumerate anatomy and assign each active limb to a visible contact target.
examples.when_to_use: Octopus typing, complex hand interactions, multi-tool operation, or any contact-heavy creature scene.
examples.why_it_matters: The best octopus anatomy appeared in radial rear views, while humanoid hybrids, reduced limb counts, and hovering tentacles failed typing credibility.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Interaction Contact Map with limb count, target device, contact state, and negative anatomy constraints.

examples.rule: For mystery prompts, explicitly separate camera platform from visible objects.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt using phrases like drone shot, handheld shot, or crane shot.
examples.why_it_matters: Several city renders literalized drone shot into visible drones instead of treating it as camera language.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Camera-language compiler that tags camera terms as non-diegetic unless the user asks for an object.

examples.rule: For premium product shots, lock one hero object's geometry and add motion through a slow camera axis or a simple material layer such as steam.
examples.when_to_use: Coffee equipment, food products, containers, and tabletop product films.
examples.why_it_matters: The moka pot and active pour-over stayed clean because the object did not transform while camera or steam supplied progression.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Stable Hero Product Mode

examples.rule: For premium transformation shots, constrain the render to one subject, one axis of change, and one visual payoff.
examples.when_to_use: AI activation, eye opening, product reveal, magical awakening, or other short hero transformations.
examples.why_it_matters: The clean eye renders maintained anatomy and framing because the only major change was eyelid opening plus iris illumination; the noisier digital-eye version changed style and geometry simultaneously.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Single-beat transformation template with locked subject, camera, lighting direction, and change axis.

examples.rule: For regulated or precision domains, prompt for a demonstration gesture but forbid invented labels, anatomy diagrams, product controls, and clinical claims.
examples.when_to_use: Healthcare, biometric, aviation, and other precision-sensitive product demonstrations.
examples.why_it_matters: Clinical posters, device forms, biometric identity, and aircraft mechanics showed visually plausible but unreliable detail.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Precision Domain mode with claim suppression, reference-required controls, and mandatory human review.

examples.rule: For rigid branded products, lock one immutable product identity before adding camera movement: exact dial color, hand count and pivot, index map, case geometry, bracelet type, and approved text.
examples.when_to_use: Watches, instruments, vehicles, devices, and any product whose value depends on mechanical precision or exact branding.
examples.why_it_matters: The best static watch renders preserved silhouette, while moving or loosely specified variants changed dial color, hands, bezel marks, model text, or bracelet construction.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Product Identity Lock with reference-frame, immutable-geometry, and exact-copy fields.

examples.rule: For time-based hero shots, restate the hero object's identity, position, material, and required visibility at every beat.
examples.when_to_use: Any prompt where a product or food hero must survive a multi-stage action.
examples.why_it_matters: The watch, submerged ring, and lifted pizza slice disappear or become unreadable after otherwise strong opening frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Persistent Hero Anchor that carries subject invariants into every generated beat.

examples.rule: For transformations, specify visible material states and a final proof frame instead of abstract quality language.
examples.when_to_use: Food, beverage, beauty, manufacturing, and craft-process prompts.
examples.why_it_matters: Beans-to-truffle, grapes-to-cognac, and ingredients-to-pasta remained legible because each state had a distinct material and endpoint.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Material-State Ladder fields for source, process states, finish, and proof frame.

examples.rule: For workplace-relief stories, specify one visible emotional transition and one physically simple gesture before adding a product beat.
examples.when_to_use: Human-led office lifestyle clips where stress, anticipation, or relief must read within five seconds.
examples.why_it_matters: Single-gesture arcs produced the most coherent acting in this batch, while compound hand, phone, hair, and product actions accumulated contact errors.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Gesture-complexity budget that warns when a short shot combines multiple hand contacts and prop interactions.

examples.rule: Generate a short shot ladder with one job per shot.
examples.when_to_use: Automotive, fashion, beauty, product, and other commercial sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Exterior-detail-interior-result ladders produced clearer coverage than long prose that mixed optics, physics, sound, cost, and narrative in one block.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Shot-ladder composer with wide, detail, interaction, result, and end-card modules.

examples.rule: Generate clean plates without readable packaging, chalk copy, signage, logos, or promotional overlays; inject verified text assets after render.
examples.when_to_use: Brand ads, cafe interiors, tutorials, benefit cards, package shots, menus, and campaign CTAs.
examples.why_it_matters: Hero text repeatedly became gibberish, misspelled, or temporally unstable and often occupied the largest visual area.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Verified Asset Layer for logos, packages, signage, menu copy, and CTA typography.

examples.rule: Generate clean visual plates and add exact copy, logos, labels, and UI in a deterministic compositor lane.
examples.when_to_use: Any brand-sensitive commercial, package shot, end card, logo alignment, phone UI, or text-removal task.
examples.why_it_matters: Generated lettering repeatedly mutated or became gibberish even when the underlying imagery was commercially strong.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Brand-safe overlay stage with mask, tracking, font, logo, and package-label locks.

examples.rule: Give a 15-second render one dominant action spine and no more than five visually distinct beats.
examples.when_to_use: Product mechanisms, food transformations, and short ritual films.
examples.why_it_matters: The cleanest renders completed a simple material or mechanical progression, while overloaded briefs dropped locations, characters, and transitions.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat Budget validator that warns when a 15-second brief exceeds five state changes or one primary action.

examples.rule: Give every five-second shot a measurable motion source: one camera move, one subject action, or one material effect.
examples.when_to_use: Scenic landscapes, illustrated tableaux, atmosphere, and product b-roll.
examples.why_it_matters: Several attractive stills failed as video because only flare, bloom, or negligible drift changed.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Motion Floor Gate

examples.rule: Give every rapid-montage beat one concrete subject, one action and one emotional verb.
examples.when_to_use: Life montages, day-in-the-life edits and multi-environment brand films.
examples.why_it_matters: Distinct action-emotion beats produced legible variety; vague overload prompts collapsed into repeated bedrooms, empty frames or narrow routine coverage.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Montage Diversity planner scoring subject, location, scale, palette, action and emotion distance between adjacent beats.

examples.rule: Give static product shots one explicit micro-motion carrier and hold every hero prop fixed.
examples.when_to_use: Coffee cups, ingredient macros, packaging, and other still-life loops.
examples.why_it_matters: Steam produced convincing motion when cups and props stayed stable, while bean and sack sequences read as five-second stills.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Micro-motion selector for steam, condensation, light drift, camera push, or ingredient movement.

examples.rule: In dense urban scenes, choose one primary subject and one transaction while explicitly suppressing readable signage and de-emphasizing background faces.
examples.when_to_use: Street markets, cafes, crowds, and travel b-roll.
examples.why_it_matters: Tracking energy remained convincing, but crowd identities, signs, hands, and small props repeatedly drifted under scene density.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Scene Density Budget with primary-subject, background-face, and signage controls.

examples.rule: In facial macro shots, lock iris size, eye spacing, nose-to-eye proportions, and skin-texture treatment across the move.
examples.when_to_use: Beauty, eye, skin, and identity-critical human close-ups.
examples.why_it_matters: High still-frame detail masked eye-size and facial-proportion drift across the sampled sequence.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Face Macro Geometry Lock

examples.rule: In tilt-shift cities, prioritize stable architecture and one traffic corridor; cap close crowd density.
examples.when_to_use: Urban dioramas with aerial, orbital, or street-level movement.
examples.why_it_matters: Buildings and road geometry held better than pedestrians, cars, signage, and crowded storefront detail.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Entity-density guard with separate architecture, traffic, crowd, and text budgets.

examples.rule: Keep critical text, UI, labels, and logos out of generative pixels unless a post-composite text layer is available.
examples.when_to_use: Packshots, phone screens, watches, jerseys, end cards, vehicle plates, and branded product advertising.
examples.why_it_matters: Critical copy frequently became gibberish, drifted between frames, or leaked an unintended real brand.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Text-safe mode that reserves clean plates and emits deterministic overlay instructions.

examples.rule: Keep crowds as atmosphere and lock one foreground anchor; do not require many readable faces or changing hand actions in the same shot.
examples.when_to_use: Markets, contests, events, cafes, and any busy public environment.
examples.why_it_matters: Crowd-heavy scenes preserved architecture and event energy but accumulated face, identity, prop, and hand continuity failures.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Crowd-risk router that reduces face prominence, selects one anchor subject, and recommends shorter shots.

examples.rule: Keep each short render to one camera progression and one primary action unless explicit cuts are requested.
examples.when_to_use: Five-second clips with character, location, and prop requirements.
examples.why_it_matters: Multi-beat prompts frequently collapsed one beat, while focused suitcase actions and explicit grind-to-pour cuts retained stronger coverage.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prompt beat-budget estimator

examples.rule: Lead with a human problem or social tension before the product hero.
examples.when_to_use: Lifestyle automotive, premium goods and feature-led comedy.
examples.why_it_matters: The strongest product narratives made the benefit legible before revealing the vehicle or control surface.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Problem-Trigger-Benefit-Payoff narrative preset with product reveal timing control.

examples.rule: Lead with observable subject, action, state change, and payoff; treat camera specifications as support rather than the prompt core.
examples.when_to_use: Food process, travel montage, character reveal, and other short-form sequences that must read from sparse sampled frames.
examples.why_it_matters: The strongest renders clearly expressed a visible progression, while many specification-heavy prompts produced one attractive but nearly static image.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prompt compiler with required Subject, Action, State Change, and Payoff fields before optional camera metadata.

examples.rule: Limit a five-second render to one primary action and one camera move; route compound narratives to an explicit shot list.
examples.when_to_use: Use whenever a prompt contains multiple characters, action transitions, or more than two temporal beats.
examples.why_it_matters: The renderer repeatedly preserved setting and palette while collapsing requested montages, activation sequences, and coordinated ensembles into one polished tableau.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat-budget validator that warns when action count exceeds duration capacity.

examples.rule: Limit each generated shot to one visually atomic physical action with a stable source object and destination object.
examples.when_to_use: Ingredient pours, storage actions, cup handling, and hands-only preparation inserts.
examples.why_it_matters: The cleanest procedural examples used one gravity-driven action, while multi-function tools and transformations produced material and mechanism failures.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Atomic Action mode with source, action, destination, and prohibited-state-change fields.

examples.rule: Limit each generation unit to one hero subject, one action, one environment, and one lighting strategy; split additional beats into separate shots.
examples.when_to_use: Prompts containing multiple locations, timestamp blocks, camera transitions, identity requirements, text, and effects.
examples.why_it_matters: Concise single-image concepts preserved composition and material quality; overloaded launch and assembly prompts dropped workers, identity, text, attire, and assembly causality.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prompt complexity budget with automatic shot splitting and explicit dropped-constraint warnings.

examples.rule: Limit short-form concept films to a small, inspectable number of scale or symbolism transitions.
examples.when_to_use: Powers-of-Ten, life-cycle, visual-rhyme, and other abstract sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Five concrete scale anchors read clearly; twelve levels or ten symbolic cuts exceeded what sampled frames could prove and introduced ambiguous transitions.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Concept Complexity Budget

examples.rule: Lock cast identity, wardrobe, and hero props across every camera move and scene transition.
examples.when_to_use: Wide-to-close human ads, testimonials, festival transitions, and lifestyle sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Camera moves and overlays sometimes concealed identity, wardrobe, cup, or package substitutions.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Continuity lock sheet for cast, wardrobe, prop inventory, and final-frame state.

examples.rule: Lock hero geometry and cap background actor count when using miniature-worker scale contrast.
examples.when_to_use: Use for dioramas, factories, crowds, technicians, or repeated small figures around one hero object.
examples.why_it_matters: Large robot heroes stayed coherent while small workers, tools, terminals, and repeated figures drifted or disappeared.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Hero-lock plus actor-count complexity control.

examples.rule: Lock hero-object silhouette, layer thickness, garnish footprint, and support contact before adding orbit, rotation, or push-in language.
examples.when_to_use: Macro food and sculptural single-object product shots.
examples.why_it_matters: Several individually polished confection frames morphed corners, layers, or silver garnish during apparent camera movement.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Temporal Object Lock block for immutable silhouette and material constraints.

examples.rule: Lock identity-changing attributes explicitly, including eyewear, face, wardrobe, vehicle model, grille, wheel, and stripe geometry.
examples.when_to_use: Continuous portraits, talking heads, hero vehicles, or any recurring subject across montage beats.
examples.why_it_matters: A founder acquired glasses mid-shot and several hero vehicles changed body details or model identity.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Continuity lock panel with immutable human and vehicle attribute slots.

examples.rule: Lock miniature cast count, wardrobe, tool assignment, and task role before adding ensemble motion.
examples.when_to_use: Tiny chefs, mechanics, station crowds, and miniature builders.
examples.why_it_matters: Large machines and food could remain stable while tiny people changed identity, anatomy, count, or tool contact.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Ensemble continuity ledger with named workers, fixed count, wardrobe swatches, and owned tools.

examples.rule: Lock product geometry and subject pose separately.
examples.when_to_use: Turntables, furniture, pet products, jewelry, and adjacent product variants.
examples.why_it_matters: The sapphire ring held geometry through angle changes, while one pet bed changed rim shape and failed to prove levitation; a second bed preserved both air gap and silhouette.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Product invariant sheet for silhouette, dimensions, support state, surface seams, pose, and allowed camera change.

examples.rule: Lock product identity attributes before asking for multi-angle coverage.
examples.when_to_use: Watches, vehicles, bottles, and other recognizable products.
examples.why_it_matters: Clean orbital renders preserved dial, case, paint, and body geometry; weaker variants changed logos, crowns, wings, mirrors, or color between angles.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity Lock block for silhouette, color, logo policy, material, component count, and forbidden drift.

examples.rule: Lock product identity explicitly: exact spelling, placement, package silhouette, window geometry, and no unprompted logo or wardrobe branding.
examples.when_to_use: Branded architecture, umbrellas, coffee packages, logos, or any product whose identity must remain stable across frames.
examples.why_it_matters: The factory name failed, one coffee bag morphed into a different package, and umbrella variants ranged from corrupted text to a stable HALO mark.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity Lock block with literal brand text, approved placement mask, silhouette reference, and reject-on-change rule.

examples.rule: Long surreal prompts should be compiled into subject, wardrobe, environment, light, and motion layers.
examples.when_to_use: Human VFX, fantasy portrait, ritual, dream, and symbolic prompts.
examples.why_it_matters: The bioluminescent prompt preserved its motif system when the layers were all visually legible.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Layered prompt compiler with visible-subject checklist and motif carryover checks.

examples.rule: Make the distinctive scale subject mandatory and repeat its physical relationship to the hero surface.
examples.when_to_use: Miniature-chef, miniature-worker, or giant-object concepts.
examples.why_it_matters: Several attractive renders silently replaced tiny agents with full-size hands, moved workers beside the target, or broke the scale hierarchy.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Scale Relationship Lock

examples.rule: Make watermark-free delivery a gold eligibility prerequisite.
examples.when_to_use: Every render intended for reuse, training exemplars, public release, or brand work.
examples.why_it_matters: All 50 reviewed videos contained a lower-right generated mark, making otherwise strong variants unsuitable as clean exemplars.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Watermark detector and clean-master eligibility gate

examples.rule: Name ambiguous luminous objects by function and material, including their source, endpoint, and interaction.
examples.when_to_use: Portal, beam, liquid, exhaust, blank-canvas, and cosmic-anomaly scenes.
examples.why_it_matters: Several attractive frames remained semantically UNKNOWN because a white plane or stream had no stable physical role.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Semantic anchor fields for object type, source, destination, material behavior, and interaction.

examples.rule: Name dish-defining geometry and ingredients, not only heat, gloss, or appetite adjectives.
examples.when_to_use: Regional food generation, especially dosa, naan, samosa, biryani, and paneer.
examples.why_it_matters: Many frames were glossy but semantically wrong: dosa became a dotted cone, naan resembled bubbling pizza, and samosa became shell-like or ravioli-like.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Dish Fidelity Guard with canonical shape, thickness, texture, garnish, and prohibited-look fields.

examples.rule: Never ask the video model to invent final packaging typography; require a supplied label asset, a blank label, or an explicit no-readable-text guard.
examples.when_to_use: Any branded product, container, monitor graphic, or packshot workflow.
examples.why_it_matters: Coffee labels repeatedly mutated into MUMCAFE, MUME CAFE, AANVI variants, and unreadable fine print across frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Brand-text lock with label-image upload, OCR diff, and automatic fallback to unbranded packaging.

examples.rule: Never ask the video model to render delivery-critical brand names, headlines, countdowns, or watch-dial text; request a clean text-free plate and composite typography afterward.
examples.when_to_use: Use whenever exact spelling, logo fidelity, or legally controlled brand presentation matters.
examples.why_it_matters: Prominent generated text was consistently corrupted, including MILION STUDIO, MILLION DILLAR STUDIO, and malformed emotional-coherence warnings.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Text-safe render mode that strips text instructions into a post-production overlay manifest.

examples.rule: Never rely on generative rendering for exact URLs, slogans, brand names, or interface copy; reserve a clean compositing pass.
examples.when_to_use: Any commercial frame with exact text or product branding.
examples.why_it_matters: Every VoltaBean URL mutated, social CTAs became gibberish, and watch dial names drifted.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Text-safe mode that generates a clean plate plus compositor text specification.

examples.rule: Never request dry beans, powder, milk, or brewed coffee to transform states inside one continuous shot.
examples.when_to_use: Coffee origin stories, brewing demos, ingredient-to-result transitions, and product preparation sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Multiple renders turned beans into liquid, materialized cups, or violated volume conservation.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Material-state guard that forces a hard cut between solid, ground, brewed, and finished-beverage beats.

examples.rule: Prefer a small number of testable beats over dense numerical choreography specifications.
examples.when_to_use: Short action clips and camera-intensive sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: The highly specified garage-fight prompt delivered the setting and mood but not reliable contact, identity, framing, or beat continuity.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Beat Budget And Complexity Warning

examples.rule: Prefer label-free material and silhouette studies when exact brand assets are unavailable; make grain, seams, facets, and light behavior the subject instead of inventing typography.
examples.when_to_use: Luxury mood films, early product exploration, and generic material advertising.
examples.why_it_matters: The cleanest luxury outputs were the unbranded black leather macro and geometric glass bottle, while labeled products repeatedly failed.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Brand Asset Missing route that defaults to label-free material cinema.

examples.rule: Prefer object-to-process-to-payoff language for food, beverage, and craft sequences.
examples.when_to_use: Transformation, ritual, process, and premium product stories.
examples.why_it_matters: Concrete milestone nouns held continuity better than abstract cinematic directives.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Transformation Arc preset with start, process, proof, and payoff fields.

examples.rule: Prefer one dominant transformation axis per shot and keep the hero grounded when geometric identity matters.
examples.when_to_use: Product rotations, macro reveals, turntables, and construction studies.
examples.why_it_matters: Grounded watch dolly-ins were materially more stable than floating rotations that morphed into bracelet loops.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Geometry-risk router that recommends grounded dolly over free rotation

examples.rule: Prefer one hero subject, one primary action, one camera axis, and one motivated light transition per shot.
examples.when_to_use: Apparel, macro nature, product reveals, and any clip where temporal coherence matters more than montage breadth.
examples.why_it_matters: The cleanest renders stayed coherent when every visible constraint could be tested in the sampled frames.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Constrained Shot Builder with subject, action, camera-axis, and light-transition slots

examples.rule: Prefer one monotonic material transition over several simultaneous physics events in a 10-second macro.
examples.when_to_use: Liquids, viscous food, aerosol, melting, cutting, and impact prompts.
examples.why_it_matters: The honey strand, atomizer mist, and whisky fill remain coherent, while crown splash, chocolate melt, and truffle shaving reset or morph.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Physics Complexity Meter with a warning when multiple irreversible material events share one shot.

examples.rule: Prefer one visible action beat with a stable subject, stable prop, and stable environment over multi-action improvisation.
examples.when_to_use: Product, hospitality, fashion, family, and service shots under five seconds.
examples.why_it_matters: The cleanest human and product renders focused on one action: adjust goggles, place a plate, settle cream, cradle an infant, or reveal an object.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Single-Beat Action composer with subject, prop, environment, and end-state locks.

examples.rule: Prefer rigid single-subject motion for reliability: orbit, profile reveal, lateral slide, or static-camera pass.
examples.when_to_use: Use for product silhouettes, aircraft, and mechanical macros where temporal coherence matters more than narrative complexity.
examples.why_it_matters: Simple rotations, slides, and overhead passes preserved geometry better than multi-actor or deformable-material sequences.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Reliability-first motion preset library.

examples.rule: Prefer short, occlusion-safe hand actions and avoid long reaches, floating cup contact, or multi-object manipulation.
examples.when_to_use: Human food preparation, sipping, product pickup, and tabletop demos.
examples.why_it_matters: Long reaches stretched anatomy and cup-to-mouth actions lost hand contact, while simple pours and cradling gestures were more stable.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Hand Interaction risk setting with low-risk grip, pour, cradle, and set-down presets.

examples.rule: Promote character, vehicle, wardrobe, color, and count locks into a compact repeated lock block for every beat.
examples.when_to_use: Multi-beat human or automotive sequences and any scene with a single hero asset.
examples.why_it_matters: Duplicate executives, beard/mustache drift, orange-to-black vehicle morphing, and green-to-silver vehicle substitution were common despite detailed prose.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Persistent Asset Lock block with count, color, wardrobe, facial-hair, and silhouette constraints

examples.rule: Prompt process stories as start, transformation, proof and resolved result.
examples.when_to_use: Food, craft, manufacturing and product assembly content.
examples.why_it_matters: The scallop, handbag and Lamborghini manufacturing sequences read as complete stories because each sampled stage changed state and ended on a clear result.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Process Story generator with mandatory before, action, proof and payoff frames.

examples.rule: Reduce miniature-workforce prompts to one hero task, two to four workers, explicit support surfaces, and locked worker count; do not combine assembly, celebration, pullback, tools, and dozens of figures in one short generation.
examples.when_to_use: Miniature dioramas, tiny-worker food scenes, cleanroom assembly, and any multi-agent macro concept.
examples.why_it_matters: Worker anatomy, count, tools, platforms, and placement repeatedly morphed when the prompt demanded too many simultaneous micro-actions.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Multi-Actor Complexity Budget with count lock, support-surface requirement, and one-action limit.

examples.rule: Reference-lock exact products and characters across every shot; repeat immutable identity and component constraints at shot level.
examples.when_to_use: Luxury goods, automotive, recurring protagonists, and branded hardware.
examples.why_it_matters: Bag accessories, watch complications, vehicle fascia, badges, and human identity drifted across multi-shot prompts.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Identity and Product Reference Lock panel

examples.rule: Reject analysis, code, framework discussion, and assistant preamble before render routing.
examples.when_to_use: Every imported or generated prompt.
examples.why_it_matters: Two 21k-character framework discussions produced unrelated, nearly static car shots with no scene-level adherence target.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prompt Hygiene Classifier

examples.rule: Reject or split concatenated prompts that contain conflicting scene clauses.
examples.when_to_use: Prompt lint detects sentence fragments, duplicated scene nouns, or an abrupt subject/domain switch.
examples.why_it_matters: The snowy-village prompts splice winter serenity and a skateboarding kitten into one malformed sentence, leaving priority ambiguous.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Compiler lint with split, choose-primary-clause, and block controls.

examples.rule: Reject repeated boilerplate or prompts whose scene payload is empty after a scene marker.
examples.when_to_use: Before dispatching long technical prompts.
examples.why_it_matters: Three dinosaur renders came from prompts that repeated camera setup and never supplied a concrete scene after 'The scene depicts:'.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Prompt-corruption lint for repetition ratio, empty scene clauses, and missing subject/action nouns.

examples.rule: Render textless plates when exact copy, UI labels, logos, packaging, URLs, or product dial markings matter; composite exact assets after render.
examples.when_to_use: Brand reveals, software demos, CTA cards, packaged goods, captions, watches, and vehicle badges.
examples.why_it_matters: Generated copy repeatedly corrupted single words, URLs, workflow labels, package copy, and dial markings even in otherwise polished footage.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Deterministic Typography and Packshot Compositor

examples.rule: Repeat scale, orientation, identity, and role-color anchors inside every shot beat rather than stating them once in an opening paragraph.
examples.when_to_use: Use for miniature workers, giant subjects, multi-role teams, and any wide-to-close sequence.
examples.why_it_matters: Miniature workers repeatedly became full-size, androids switched from horizontal to vertical, and named specialists disappeared after camera transitions.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Per-shot invariant pins for subject identity, relative scale, orientation, count, and role color.

examples.rule: Replace protected character names with licensed or original character descriptors unless explicit IP use is authorized.
examples.when_to_use: Commercial superhero, celebrity, logo, or branded-character prompts.
examples.why_it_matters: The Mumbai variants visibly reproduced a protected web-slinging character and inherited brand-leakage risk.
examples.os_feature_candidate: IP-risk linter with original-character rewrite.

examples.rule: Represent rapid editorial montages as an explicit shot list with hard-cut boundaries and one identity/prop state per shot.
examples.when_to_use: When the prompt requests different people, colors, or products in sub-second shots.
examples.why_it_matters: The four colorful-coffee renders produced one continuous person and morphing mug rather than distinct cuts.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Cut-aware montage composer

examples.rule: Require an observable state change whenever the user asks for melting, reacting, falling, opening, scoring, or transforming.
examples.when_to_use: Any action-led shot or short-form beat.
examples.why_it_matters: Several clean frames failed as video because the requested action never materially progressed.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Action Proof field that defines start state, midpoint change, and end state before generation.

examples.rule: Require the named subject to perform the named verb; ambient steam, door movement, or light ripples do not satisfy action.
examples.when_to_use: Food, product, macro, and character prompts where the action is the point of the shot.
examples.why_it_matters: Several chef and coffee variants looked polished but only steam moved, and one synthetic eye remained a static lens study without activation.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Subject-Verb Motion Contract with static-action rejection

examples.rule: Require visible intermediate states for transformations and mechanical processes.
examples.when_to_use: Dissolves, assembly, brewing, food processing, and miniature-machine sequences.
examples.why_it_matters: Without an explicit visible mechanism, renders substituted abrupt state swaps, static completed objects, or decorative machinery.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Transformation-state planner with before/contact/intermediate/after proof frames.

examples.rule: Require visible intrinsic motion for illustrated or still-life concepts; a static image or digital zoom alone does not pass video QC.
examples.when_to_use: Illustration, nature still life, character art, and product tableaux.
examples.why_it_matters: Woodblock waves, forest acorns, and the cartoon cow delivered little or no subject motion, while water ripples and Ferris-wheel rotation created valid temporal evidence.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Motion Evidence gate requiring a declared moving subject, material, environment, or mechanism.

examples.rule: Reserve readable copy for controlled packshots and validate it as a separate deliverable.
examples.when_to_use: End cards, product names, URLs, lap telemetry, dashboards and signage.
examples.why_it_matters: CarryOn and the final HydraTrack card were usable; lap timers, dial text, plates and intermediate logos often became gibberish.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Text-Safe End Card mode with OCR gate and fallback to textless render plus deterministic overlay.

examples.rule: Resolve output aspect ratio as a hard render contract before adding lens, camera, or grading detail.
examples.when_to_use: Every prompt, especially cinematic-master prompts that request 2.39:1 or 16:9.
examples.why_it_matters: Sixteen reviewed renders were delivered in portrait despite explicit widescreen instructions; technical verbosity did not protect the most basic format constraint.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Aspect Contract preflight that blocks generation when requested and provider output ratios disagree.

examples.rule: Route exact brand and title requirements to a deterministic graphics or compositing lane.
examples.when_to_use: A prompt requests a real logo, product listing, or exact title text.
examples.why_it_matters: Both workbook ads produced misspelled brand text and failed the requested title despite otherwise usable lifestyle imagery.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Exact-text overlay contract with generated clean-plate background.

examples.rule: Route exact brand and title text through a typography-safe render mode or post-composite layer.
examples.when_to_use: Logos, title cards, UI labels, percentages, and any exact spelling requirement.
examples.why_it_matters: Text-only prompting succeeded once, but integrated signs and dashboards repeatedly generated misspellings, gibberish, and impossible values.
examples.os_feature_candidate: Exact-text compositor and OCR gate.
